If you throw an object up into the air in a moving car, why doesn't it go flying backwards? This gets to the heart of Newton's Laws of Motion. Although many of us engineers and other technical folks take them for granted, now, they really did go against people's common sense intuition. Living in an environment like we do, where friction is ever-present, many people intuitively feel that a force must be continuously applied to an object for it to continue moving. Newton's insight can be summed up in his famous first law (copied here from Wikipedia’s paraphrase): A body remains at rest, or in motion at a constant speed in a straight line, except insofar as it is acted upon by a force. The reason why objects in our everyday lives always slow down is because they're always subjected to external forces that slow them down, namely friction and air resistance. If it wasn't for those external forces, once you started an object in motion, it would continue moving forever, or at least until some other force acted upon it. So, when you're riding along in a car, the car, you, and any other objects in the car are all moving along at some speed. Let's just say 60 mph for the sake of argument. So, if you throw an object up inside the car, what force is going to slow it down? All the air in the car is traveling along with you at that same 60 mph, so there won't be any drag. Nothing else is touching the object to impart friction. So there isn't any force in the horizontal direction to slow the object down, and it'll continue right along at that 60 mph. Now, in the vertical direction, you did throw the object up to begin with, which gave it a starting force and corresponding vertical speed. And then the force of gravity will continuously pull it down, which will initially slow its upward speed, and eventually result in an ever increasing downward speed until you catch it again. Assuming this object is something hefty enough to ignore the small amount of air resistance (i.e. not a feather), after it leaves your hand, the only significant force would be gravity. So if we were to draw what's known as a free body diagram, it would look like this: So, with a force in only one direction, that's the only direction in which speed will change. Now, if we threw the object out the window instead of keeping it inside the car, that's a whole different story. Ignoring any wind, the air outside the car is essentially motionless. So as soon as the object hits that air, there will be air resistance. Now, the object will have at least two forces acting on it – the air resistance and the gravity. So now, the object will change speed in both the vertical and horizontal directions. Gravity will pull it downwards, while the air resistance will slow it down relative to the car. So from your perspective in the car, it will go flying backwards. But, just to point out one more thing, consider it from the point of view of somebody standing by the side of the road watching you. When you threw the object out the window, they wouldn't see it go flying backwards. They would see you, the car, and the object all initially at 60 mph. Then, the object would slow down while you and the car kept on going at 60 mph. You'd all be moving forward, it's just that you and the car would be going faster than the object. The figure below is about dropping a bomb, but it shows basically the same thing: ABOVE: Notice the difference between the ‘Vacuum Trajectory’ (with no drag) vs. the ‘Actual Trajectory’ (with drag) SOURCE: CHAPTER-23-D Basically, the reason an object tossed in a car doesn't go flying backwards is because it was already moving at the same speed as you and the car, and there's no force to change that.

If someone was hypothetically able to view the light that left Earth 65 million years ago during the Cretaceous period, what would they see and witness? I assume you picked 65 million years hoping to see dinosaurs. But in reality, you’re going to see something like this: ABOVE SOURCE: Jwst Feed (@jwstfeed.bsky.social) Yes, that’s an entire galaxy, not a single solar system, let alone a single planet like Earth. That is the galaxy known as NGC 3972, which is around 60–65 million light years away. This image was captured with the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), which is one of the most powerful telescopes ever built. Here’s another photo of the same galaxy by another incredibly powerful telescope, Hubble: ABOVE SOURCE: NGC 3972 - Wikipedia The issue is that 65 million light years is a long way away. The other issue is that telescopes can only ‘magnify’ an image so much. Because of the wave nature of light, as opposed to being pure rays, there’s essentially a limit to how much you can focus the image depending on how big your mirror is. That in turn limits how much detail you can make out. It’s not an issue of cramming a higher resolution scanner into your telescope. That would just give you a higher resolution of an out of focus image. I’ve gone through the math before in other answers. But if you wanted to make out a triceratops to roughly the resolution shown below from 65 million light years away, you would need a telescope 260 light years in diameter. That’s not gonna happen. Even solar gravitational lens telescope proposals only increase the effective diameter to that of a star, which is still well short of 260 light years. (That’s Galileo in the bottom right for scale, by the way.) The other issue that people tend not to think about is exposure times. If you look up the image info for NGC 3972 at HubbleSite.org, it lists exposure dates from April - July, 2015. Now, I’m not sure if it was focused on that single galaxy for the entire time. But still, you’re looking at a long exposure time to generate such an image. So if you were hoping to see individual dinosaurs, they’re not going to sit still that long for a portrait. Basically, with any type of realistic telescope technology, the best your going to do is a nice picture of the Milky Way galaxy. Maybe you’ll be able to pick out the Sun, but trying to image Earth on it’s own, let alone in any detail to see individual animals, just ain’t gonna happen. Related answers:

‘After-birth abortion’: Are they serious? Well, if you look at the actual situations where this is being discussed rather than just fear mongering about imaginary situations, then yes. Nobody wants to kill a healthy late term fetus or newborn. No woman goes through 9 months of pregnancy just to decide at the last minute that she's changed her mind. And certainly no doctor would kill a healthy newborn baby after the entire process of labor or a Caesarean delivery. But not all fetuses and newborns are healthy. Hopefully, with good pre-natal care, any major complications will be detected early. But not everybody has access to the best pre-natal care, and even then, some complications simply don't get detected until late into the pregnancy. And some of these complications are euphemistically referred to as "incompatible with life". In other words, they're complications so severe that the baby won't survive even with the best medical treatment available. Trying to treat these conditions will only delay the inevitable and prolong the suffering. So, the question becomes, what truly is the most humane and merciful course of action in these cases? Prolonging suffering, or doing what you can to ease the pain and try to end the suffering as soon as possible? In another recent answer, Jeff Lewis's answer to Democrats support post-birth abortion, but isn’t abortion after birth just murder?, I discussed a study that polled "physicians and paramedical professionals involved in late TOP [termination of pregnancy] decision‐making in all eight centers with a Neonatal Intensive Care Unit in Flanders, Belgium (N = 117)". As I pointed out in that answer, "These aren't folks for whom this question is a mere hypothetical. They have to see the consequences and suffering of the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit on a daily basis." And such health care professionals were overwhelmingly in favor of "actively terminat[ing] life" for newborns with serious enough conditions. And while the support for feticide wasn't quite so overwhelming, a majority still supported feticide over palliative care in serious enough cases. So yes, sometimes the humane and merciful choice is to end a poor newborn's suffering. It's a tragedy, and would be absolutely gut wrenching to the parents (and the doctors – they're humans, too). But the alternative is just forcing the newborn to suffer longer before still eventually dying. Seriously, these are profound and extremely serious situations that some families find themselves in. Let's not take away the merciful options in an already shitty situation just so we can shout some slogans to win political points. ETA: After some feedback in the comments, I want to be very clear on this. I'm talking about newborns with severe complications and no chance of recovery. The question is what’s best for these babies, which has to be looked at on a case by case basis. Is there any quality of life at all, or just suffering? Palliative care and hospice are already available for newborns with severe complications, ranging from not attempting to treat the condition, to withholding nutrition. And quite obviously, such infants will die. But with their condition, they would have died anyway. It certainly can't be considered more humane to prolong their suffering. And that leads into the debate raised in this question, although the OP seemed disingenuous in how they framed it, of whether active feticide is an appropriate approach for these babies, or if the current standard of palliative care is sufficient (and I really, really hope you're not against palliative care – who would actually push for making babies suffer even more). As I said in my prior answer, "I understand people's hesitancy to enable doctor's to actively end the life of patients as opposed to mere palliative care, especially in the case of patients who are too young to voice their own desires." So the question comes down to balancing the best interests of babies with such severe complications vs. how comfortable we are with intentionally taking steps to end a life. Minimizing the suffering for these babies as much as possible would require active feticide. Palliative care allows people to have an easier conscience, but forces the babies to suffer a bit longer. Active attempts to treat such conditions would prolong the suffering the longest. And as I pointed out in my answer, these aren't just hypotheticals. There are real, non-thought experiment babies suffering in NICUs right now, with parents agonizing over their decisions.

If you see an iPhone in the dessert, you'd say someone created it. Why can't the same be said for humans? I've gotta admit – although I've come across Paley's watchmaker analogy plenty of times, thinking about it just now in terms of an iPhone really drove home just how silly of an argument it is. We know exactly how iPhones are made. We can go visit the factories where they're built, or the engineering offices where they're designed. There's a direct trail of evidence to understanding that they're human artifacts. ABOVE SOURCE: Inside Apple's iPhone Factory We also know how people get 'made' (sorry, but I can't include a picture of that one on a family site). There are no factories or engineers involved (well, outside of engineers having kids the old fashioned way). If I come across a human in a desert, I would suspect that they were conceived, born, and raised in the natural way, not that they were some sort of artificial creation. If you want to argue that people are some sort of engineered beings, show the evidence of the factories and designers the same way we can for an iPhone. What's more, beyond the way that individual people are conceived, we have plenty of evidence for evolution for the origin of our species as a whole. We know the mechanisms and patterns. We understand many of the genetic processes. We've found fossils showing the evolution of humans from prior ape species (and plenty of other evolutionary histories besides just us people, but I'm sticking to the topic of the question). ABOVE SOURCE: Julian Norris's answer to What is the most complete visual human evolution chart available? So if you're going to try to argue that humans are somehow engineered or designed, not only do you need to find evidence of the factories and the designers, you have to also account for all the evidence we have that currently seems to point exclusively to evolution. Were all those older hominids previous models? Did the designer(s) release upgrades every few millennia? Assuming the designer(s) designed other organisms besides just us people, why did they seem to self-impose limitations of a nested hierarchy, never taking good design improvements (like feathers or mammary glands) and using them in a different group? It would be like when GM first introduced airbags in the Oldsmobile Toronado, and that all subsequent installations of airbags would be limited to other Oldsmobiles, and never carried over to other products in GM's portfolio, and never adopted by other designers at other automakers. Basically, iPhones and biological beings are completely different things. It just seems silly to try to compare the design and manufacture of iPhones to people.

Why are people losing the movie-going habit? This is actually the future many of us dreamed of. Okay, maybe not the death of movie theaters, per se, but the conditions that are leading to the demise of theaters – big screen TVs and movies on demand from the comfort of your family room. I was a high school student in the early to mid '90s just as home computers were becoming more or less 'modern', with photo realistic images, realistic sound, video clips, online services and the Internet becoming mainstream, etc. There was talk of movies on demand eventually becoming a thing, but it seemed like distant future sci-fi. The first streaming video I remember, RealVideo from 1997, seemed like a revolution at the time (watching a video without having to download the entire file, first), but the results were impressive more for the novelty than the actual video quality. The difference between modern day Netflix and early Internet video is just astounding (I'm sure broadband Internet access is a huge contributor here). TVs and monitors have come just as far. Even in 2004, the average screen size was only 25.4", and even 'large' CRT TVs from the '90s were in the 27" - 32" range. And standard definition TV was still the standard – roughly equivalent to 640×480. A crappy stream quality on a 640x480 27" TV just isn't going to compare to watching a movie in the theaters. But with flat screen TVs, sizes and quality have exploded. The average screen size in 2019 was 47", but even 80" and bigger is now available without breaking the bank. And TVs these days come in Full HD (1920×1080), 4k (3840×2160), or even 8k (7680×4320). Those are in the ballpark of the actual projectors at movie theaters, so you're not really losing any detail watching a movie at home. So basically, we now have the ability to watch movies on demand from the comfort of our own homes, on TVs that are comparable in quality to theaters. Why are people losing the movie-going habit? Because we're living in the future. ABOVE SOURCE: reddit

What movies were marketed in a very misleading way, making the audience expect something different from what was presented? Home Alone. What it delivered was a waste of 143 minutes of my life, and a loss of childhood innocence with the realization that movies could actually be bad. I wrote about this movie not too long ago on Quora if you want my longer take on just how bad it is and why: The reason this movie holds such a place of notoriety in my mind is because it was the first time in my life I'd gone to a movie theater and regretted it. Prior to that, I'd never seen a movie that I recognized as bad. The closest were boring 'adult' movies that I knew weren't actually targeted to me, and that I might enjoy once I grew older. But kids aren't hard to please. And I was 12 years old when Home Alone was released. I was the target audience. I was even excited about going to see the movie based on the trailers and commercials, so I was shocked when I sat down to watch the full movie in its entirety, and it turned out to be so horrible. I realize this may not be exactly the type of answer you were looking for, but it was the first time in my life that I felt betrayed by movie marketing.

If a Starship without any payload can barely reach up to orbital speeds while expending almost ALL of the fuel within it, then could it be that SpaceX underestimated how easy/difficulty would be conceiving a fully reusable craft? Look, I've got my reservations about SpaceX's approach to safety with their 'Let's just blow stuff up till it quits blowing up approach'*, and I think that they can sometimes be a bit overhyped by Musk fanbois.** But let's keep things in perspective. They're a company with tons of talent from professional aerospace engineers. Even if they underestimated the difficulty of this approach back in the very beginning, by the time you're building and testing full scale prototypes, you've already gone through feasibility studies, trade studies, preliminary design, detail design, and tons and tons of analysis. The vehicle is performing more or less as predicted, and has the potential to be a truly awesome rocket once all the bugs are worked out. Look to Frank Norris's answer or Steve Baker's answer for more details, but the bottom line is that this vehicle will likely achieve its goal of delivering 100 – 150 tons of payload to orbit in the reusable configuration. That is quite an achievement. *My reservations with their 'Go-fast-fail-fast' approach is in the mindset, that if something hasn't gone wrong yet, then it must be good. That's way too reminiscent of the mindset that led to the Challenger disaster. Coming from an aviation background, myself, the standard level of safety for airliners is a probability of catastrophic failure of less than 1 per billion flight hours. You can't demonstrate that with a mere 100 flights with only around 10 minutes each getting to orbit and another 20 minutes for re-entry and landing. You either need prohibitive numbers of test flights, or you need to do lots and lots of traditional analysis. But if it takes half a dozen attempts to get even your first successful full flight, then your traditional analysis couldn't have been all that robust. On the other hand, other rocket manufacturers have plenty of failures, as well, so extreme risk in comparison to aviation just seems to be part of the game (though when Musk starts his dreaming about sending millions of people to Mars, that's when this safety approach becomes irresponsible). **In fairness, while Musk fanbois might overhype SpaceX, there are plenty of folks who go too far the other way, criticizing SpaceX too harshly merely because Musk himself seems to be a bit of a jackass. Whatever you think of Musk shouldn't detract from the real accomplishments of SpaceX. And remember, the company has many, many more engineers and technicians working there to achieve their successes.

Is it true that the shooter at Trump's rally was a registered Republican with conservative beliefs and a gun enthusiast? Why are conservatives blaming the left for this incident? There's simply not much to go on to identify his political leanings at this point. Back in 2021, when he was 17, he made a $15 donation to a progressive organization, ActBlue. And yes, despite online rumors, it most likely really was him. When he was old enough to vote, he registered as a Republican. This could mean he legitimately was a Republican. But given that Pennsylvania has a closed primary, this could also mean he wanted to participate in the Republican primary rather than the Democratic primary. As a liberal living in Texas with an open primary, I've voted in the Republican primary before, since I figured it was my only realistic option of trying to influence the governor's race (the Republican I preferred still lost). He seemed to like guns, trying out for his school's shooting team and being a member of a local gun range. At the time of the shooting, he was wearing a t-shirt for a gun enthusiast YouTube channel. But while enthusiasm for guns does skew a bit towards conservative political leanings, it's not at all a sure thing. I like taking my own pistol to the range, for example, and I know plenty of other liberals and Democrats who own and shoot guns. (I'll add that I've seen a few gun enthusiasts trying to use a No True Scotsman argument, claiming that a true gun enthusiast wouldn't have missed this shot, would have used a different rifle, etc. But you don't have to be an expert marksman to merely like guns and like going shooting.) In interviews with former classmates, one student who took an American history course with him stated that he "definitely was conservative", and went on to add about a mock debate that, "The majority of the class were on the liberal side, but Tom, no matter what, always stood his ground on the conservative side." But there's any number of reasons to take this hearsay with a grain of salt (the classmate could have been talking big just to get attention; he might not have known the shooter as well as he claimed, the shooter might have just enjoyed arguing, etc.) I'd also point out that people's political motivations can be quite fluid around that age. Whatever he believed at 17 might not be the same as at 18 or 20. And finally, as I've seen many others point out, we don't even know if his motivation was political. The guy who tried to assassinate Reagan did it to try to get the attention of a movie star. At this point, anybody claiming to know definitively one way or the other which way the shooter leaned politically is not looking at the evidence objectively. And it's an even bigger stretch to try to definitively claim that politics were his main motivation. Investigators are doing their best to figure out his motives. So until then, or until more public evidence comes to light, let's try to keep our speculations grounded in what's actually known. Update 2024–07–22: While it’s still a bit early to say anything definitive about the shooter, the emerging picture seems to be that he was looking for notoriety by shooting somebody famous, not any particular political leanings. In addition to Trump, he’d been searching online for Biden and other prominent political figures. Can airplanes sometimes not store fuel in their tanks due to weight limitations? If this is the case, what are the alternatives for storing fuel in an airplane or other vehicle? Airplanes are much more weight sensitive than the cars that most people are used to. Cars have fuel tanks that will typically let you drive somewhere around 5 hours before needing to refuel. And you don't need to worry all that much about how much you load up your car. It can be just you driving by yourself, or loading up the whole family with luggage. Your gas mileage might go down a bit, but unless you're looking at really heavy cargo, you don't have to worry about overloading the car. Planes, on the other, don't have that luxury. You get a combined 'useful load', which is how much you can load up an airplane before it becomes too heavy to fly. It's up to the operator to decide how much of that useful load to devote to passengers and other payload, and how much to devote to fuel. Take the Cessna 172 as an example, one of the most iconic general aviation airplanes. It has 4 seats, a useful load of 878 lbs, and gas tanks that can hold 318 lbs of fuel. If you're running the math in your head, you can see that if you filled up the tanks with fuel, you'd only have 560 lbs of payload left, which may be fine if you're flying by yourself, but doesn't leave a lot of weight for 4 passengers and luggage, especially if they're adults. ABOVE: A screenshot from Cessna’s website, with appropriate text for a discussion about fuel burn SOURCE: Cessna Skyhawk Piston | Textron Aviation But, that 318 lbs of fuel is enough to let you fly for over 5 hours. Do you really need to fly that long if you're just taking some friends up for a sight-seeing flight around town, or for the clichéd $100 hamburger at the next airport over? Probably not. So, you might only load up half the fuel, which still lets you fly over 2 ½ hours, but leaves you 719 lbs for passengers and other payload, which is getting much more reasonable for 4 people (not necessarily 4 large adults, but at least a mix of larger and more petit folks). It's all about giving the operator options. You could make the full fuel payload seem higher by giving them a smaller gas tank, but then they wouldn't have the freedom to fly longer flights. Or you could just give it two seats, but then they wouldn't have the freedom to carry more passengers. So, you give them the ability to decide how they want to use the plane. For the big boys in airliners, it's a lot of the same considerations. Is it a short haul flight between close cities? Only load as much fuel as you need and then cram it full of passengers. Is it a long range flight? Well, you might have to go lighter on the cargo. So to answer the question directly, yes, sometimes airplanes don't fill up the wing tanks in order to be able to carry more payload. But other times it's the opposite, filling up the tanks and carrying less payload. It's all up to the specific mission.

As a native-English-language-speaker, is there ever situation in which you actually should not speak perfectly accurate English as defined by most academically approved English grammar and vocabulary books? I do it all the time, especially depending on how pedantic of a book you’re thinking of. In fact, I did it just there in that sentence, by ending it with a preposition. Sure, most modern style guides don’t include that rule, but it was something I was taught back in grade school. Ending sentences with prepositions often just flows better than other constructions. There’s also the old rule about not splitting infinitives. It’s another one that’s growing outdated, but you can still find style guides recommending against it, such as here: But again, sentences often flow better when you split the infinitive, so I’ve got no qualms with doing so. There are also times were ‘proper’ grammar sounds stilted or pompous. For example, I know when to use ‘whom’ vs. ‘who’*, but I usually go with ‘who’, anyway, to avoid the appearance of being pretentious. In other cases, there are words or phrases that I simply avoid, because the technically accurate meaning is not the same as the common usage. So if you use it the technically accurate way, a large part of your audience won’t understand you. And if you use it the common way, the pedants will jump on you. A good example of this is ”begs the question” – it doesn’t mean what most people think it means**. There are also cases where the incorrect grammar carries a certain connotation or emotional aspect that you wouldn’t get from proper grammar. “Say it isn’t so” just doesn’t sound as good as “Say it ain’t so.” Related to that last one are informal contractions, where there actually are slightly different shades of meaning. If I ask somebody, “What are you doing?”, it carries a connotation of the actual, specific actions they’re currently engaged in. If I ask, “Whatcha doin’?”, it’s more of a general inquiry. I could go on, but hopefully that’s enough examples to make the point. You definitely don’t want to overdo it, but there are still plenty of occasions to use informal grammar that wouldn’t necessarily be approved of by your English teacher. As a note of caution from someone who’s semi-fluent in a second language, myself, you have to really know a language well before you understand the rules well enough to know when it’s appropriate to break them. If you’re learning English as a second language, it’s best to just try your best to speak it as properly as you can, at least until you’re really, really comfortable with the language and slang. (BTW – did you notice that split infinitive, there?) *The Oatmeal has a useful comic on this: ** Okay, as more of a descriptivist than a prescriptivist, ‘what it means’ is what most people think it means. But you’ll still get complaints from the pedants.

Why aren't autogyros as popular as cars? I'm not sure everyone knows exactly what an autogyro is, so let me start off with some background. Way back in the day, before practical helicopters, autogyros were the first practical rotorcraft. But unlike helicopters, the rotor isn't powered in flight. It's made to spin by aerodynamic means, technically known as autorotation. So, autogyros can't hover, and they still need a propeller or some other form of propulsion. Still, back in those early days, autogyros gave much better short field performance than airplanes, along with improved low speed handling characteristics (no stall since your ‘wings’ are rotating independently of your airspeed). As autogyro technology advanced, they even developed jump takeoff abilities, where a clutched driveshaft from the engine would spin up the rotor to a high rpm on the ground, and then increase the pitch on the blades and use that rotor inertia to jump into the air. The rotor head can still be simpler than a helicopter, and you also don’t need a tail rotor (no torque to the rotor once you’re in the air). Here’s a Pitcairn PA-36, towards the zenith of autogyro popularity before being eclipsed by helicopters, demonstrating jump takeoff and short landing capabilities: Nowadays, gyros are mostly relegated to small recreational aircraft, not quite as mechanically complex as that PA-36 up above. They split the difference between airplanes and helicopters, while remaining much less complex and less expensive than helicopters. I’ve seen ultralight gyros take off in the space of about 25 ft, and touch down vertically with no roll out. ABOVE: A typical modern recreational autogyro SOURCE: AutoGyro MT-03 - Wikipedia Anyway, on to the question of why autogyros aren't as popular as cars. First, personal aircraft in general, from airplanes to helicopters to autogyros, are never going to be as popular as cars. The training to become a pilot is more extensive and regulated than earning a driver's license. The extra rigor of aircraft certification and maintenance drives higher prices. Aircraft, even rotorcraft, can only fly between locations that can easily accommodate aircraft (i.e. no door to door from your house to the mall). And bad weather and high winds are a much bigger deal for air travel, and would ground the aircraft during storms or fog that are a mere nuisance in cars. In other words, you'll still need cars, so personal aircraft would be your second or third vehicle. As far as why autogyros are even less popular than airplanes and helicopters, it's because they fall somewhere in the middle performance-wise, so they don't perform typical rotorcraft missions as well as helicopters, or fixed-wing missions as well as airplanes. If you need to hover, you need a helicopter. And if you want to fly fast, airplanes are more efficient than most gyros. There are some companies trying to push modern day gyros if you only need short/zero roll takeoffs and landings but not full hover capability, but truth be told, the market hasn’t really embraced gyros very widely beyond personal / recreational vehicles. As an aside, there have been efforts over the years for even more advanced autogyros. Particularly well known (at least among aviation nerds) was the Fairey Rotodyne. They actually powered the rotor with tip jets for takeoff and landing, so it could hover. But then they transitioned the rotor to autorotation in flight, reducing the rpm to reduce drag and using the wings and props to fly more like an airplane. It's major drawback was that those tip jets were LOUD, though perhaps that might have been addressed had it not been for politics when Fairey was acquired by Westland Aircraft who already had a competing rotorcraft division. Anyway, it was still an interesting concept:

Is it true that Americans from the South are friendly? It depends on the context. I just finished reading Malcom Gladwell's book, Outliers. In one portion, he described an interesting series of experiments that took place in the 1990s at the University of Michigan. Young men were asked to enter a classroom to fill out a questionnaire, and then drop it off down the hallway before returning for some follow up. For half of the participants, the trip to drop off the questionnaire and return were uneventful. For the other half, a plant (as in an actor) got in their way in the narrow hallway trying to access a filing cabinet, acting annoyed when the student tried to get past, then slamming the filing cabinet drawer shut and calling the student an asshole. Upon returning to the original classroom, the researchers "shook the young men's hands to see if their grip was firmer than usual. They took saliva samples from the students, both before and after the insult, to see if being called an asshole caused their levels of testosterone and cortisol... to go up." They also had them provide a conclusion to a story about a hypothetical situation of a couple, Jill and Steve, going to a party, and another guy, Larry, hitting on Jill. The researchers looked at all types of different characteristics of their study subjects, but found the biggest predictor of their reactions to the hallway incident was where they were from. For northerners, "They laughed it off. Their handshakes were unchanged. Their levels of cortisol actually went down, as if they were unconsciously trying to defuse their own anger. Only a few of them had Steve get violent with Larry." On the other hand, "But the Southerners? Oh, my. The were angry. Their cortisol and testosterone jumped. Their handshakes got firm. Steve was all over Larry." They did follow up studies with similar scenarios, always finding that southerners typically reacted much more aggressively than did northerners. The difference is that the Southern United States has a "culture of honor", partly inherited from the immigrants who settled there (for historical reasons I won't delve into here – see Culture of honor (Southern United States) - Wikipedia ), and partly maintained throughout history. The scenarios in the above experiments were anything but 'friendly'. The southern students were much more likely to react aggressively. But in other situations, a culture of honor can lead to more formal politeness, or going out of your way to establish your reputation. The use of 'sir' and 'ma'am' is a pretty obvious one. In my experience, I've also seen many more people here in Texas stop to help a stranger stranded on the side of the road than I did growing up in Pennsylvania and Maryland. So, it depends. In some ways, the culture of honor can lead southerners to be friendly. In other ways, it can lead them to being more aggressive. It really just depends on the situation. But overall, I definitely wouldn’t say that they’re more friendly than me and my fellow Yankees. There are just different cultural norms and expectations.

Can an astronaut break the orbit if he jumps from the ISS by pushing himself towards the earth? The gravity will keep increasing. Can he reach earth's surface without burning if he uses a bit of air friction from a device? I'm not sure you really understand the magnitudes involved here. Objects in orbit aren't serenely floating in zero gravity. They're still very much under the influence of Earth's gravity, and constantly in a state of free fall. The only reason they don't hit the Earth is because they're moving so damn fast horizontally: ABOVE: An updated figure of Newton’s original explanation of orbits SOURCE: newton-cannon-orbital-types-Seeds The ISS is orbiting at 17,500 mph. It travels around the entire Earth every 90 minutes. A person can't come anywhere close to generating those speeds by shear muscle power. I saw a few physics forums that estimated that a person could jump somewhere around 5 m/s in zero g. Converting that to my antiquated American units, that's 11.2 mph. So, by jumping perpendicularly to the ISS’s path, you're changing your trajectory by an angle calculated by arcsin(11.2 mph / 17,500 mph), which works out to 0.037°. ABOVE: That change in velocity vector drawn to scale – solid black is the original vector, dashed orange is the new one. That’s not going to change your orbital path much at all. I mean, sure, that's enough to make your orbit slightly different than the ISS, but otherwise it would hardly be noticeable. If the ISS orbit were perfectly circular (which I doubt it is), this 11.2 mph difference would make your new orbit just ever so slightly elliptical, certainly too small of a difference to notice by eye. Basically, when you're already careening around the planet at 17,500 mph, the tiny difference in velocity from human muscle power is only going to have a negligible effect on your path.

Why do people go to so-called fancy restaurants that serve small average portions with insanely high prices? My wife and I have done this a handful of times for special occasions, and we really enjoyed it. My guess is you're probably thinking of dishes like these, where everything is put on the plate with an eye to detail and presentation, but the portion sizes are pretty small: ABOVE SOURCE: Sidart Introduce New Set Menu - Restaurant & Café And you may also be thinking that that's just a publicity photo of dishes at that restaurant, and that you'd only get to pick one of those plates for your meal. But these dishes are usually part of a 'tasting menu' or 'set menu', which works a bit differently than the normal restaurant routine. If you ordered the set menu at that particular restaurant that made the food in the above photo (Sidart), you'd get all of those dishes brought out to you in succession. In this case, that's 6 food courses plus a drink (probably as a palate cleanser somewhere in there), but I've heard of tasting menus with over a dozen courses. Add on your wine, and it's a decently filling meal. Sometimes they'll even offer a glass of a different wine with each course to complement each particular dish. You may not be stuffed the same way you would be after an all you can eat buffet, but it's enough food to be satisfying. And man oh man does the food taste good (at least the ones we've tried). The restaurant is really focused on attention to detail, and packing as much flavor as they can into those small portions. Think about Thanksgiving dinner, and how there are so many different dishes that you can only take a little bit of each thing – just enough to get a taste. But now, imagine that with actual chefs, preparing dishes far more involved than cheesy potato casserole, bringing each dish out to you one at a time so that each course is still freshly prepared when you take your first bite (and not having to do any of the cooking or cleaning up afterwards). On top of all that, it's an experience. The portions may be small, but going through that many individual courses still takes time. This isn't your typical hour-ish restaurant meal. Depending on exactly how many courses you're getting, expect somewhere in the 2 to 3 hour range, relaxing and enjoying the company of whoever you're with. But realize that this means the restaurant only gets your party at that table for those 2 to 3 hours, not the 2 to 3 parties they could have gotten with a more typical meal, which is part of the reason the prices are higher. It's not an everyday thing, or even a once a month thing (unless you're a lot better off than we are). But for a rare treat for a special occasion, these types of meals are very nice. Is it possible to believe in God if you are an atheist? It's not really about possibilities. It's about definitions. If you don't believe in any gods, you are, by definition, an atheist. If you do believe in any gods or deities, you are, by definition, a theist or a deist, and not an atheist. It's certainly possible for somebody who was an atheist to have a change of heart and become a theist or deist. But at that point, by definition, they cease to be an atheist. So no, a person can't be both an atheist and a believer in some god, because it's simply a contradiction in terms. But there's nothing stopping individual atheists from becoming believers (or vice versa).

Young Earth creationists like to use Bishop Ussher's calculated date for when the Earth was created. Who else has done the calculations to confirm it? I've gone through a portion of the estimate, myself*. You can read a good summary of Ussher's estimate on Wikipedia. Basically, he broke it down into three portions (note that the timespans are the ones that Ussher calculated, not mine): Ussher then used other sources outside the Bible to determine the enthronement of the Babylonian king Amel-Marduk to have occurred in 562 BC, which was tied in to the end of the Babylonian Captivity through 2 Kings 25:27. From there, it was just a matter of going backwards by all the years previously calculated, putting creation at 4004 BC. Since the first two portions of the estimate are so straightforward, they were easy enough to double check. Creation to Exodus Like I said, this part is easy enough to look up yourself in Genesis 5 and Genesis 11. The only real minor cases of uncertainty in there are when Noah had Shem, and when Nahor had Terah, since the wording used is a tad ambiguous. In the first case, per Genesis 5:32: After Noah was five hundred years old, Noah became the father of Shem, Ham, and Japheth. In the latter case, per Genesis 11:26: When Terah had lived seventy years, he became the father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran. Those sons weren't triplets, so you have to decide whether those ages are when those guys started having kids, or when they'd finally had all three. Folks who care more about this than I do (like Ussher) have tried to get to the bottom of it. I just used those numbers as is, since it's still in the ballpark. Anyway, here's my table of going from Adam to the birth of Abraham: So, it comes out to 1949 years. Next, take a look at Genesis 12:4: So Abram went, as the Lord had told him, and Lot went with him. Abram was seventy-five years old when he departed from Haran. So, Abraham was 75 years old at the start of the events in Exodus. Add those two numbers together, and you get 2024 years from the creation of Adam to the start of the events in Exodus. Ussher came up with 2082. Maybe that's to do with the aforementioned issues around Noah and Terah, or the time between the start of the events of in Exodus and actually escaping, or maybe even which source of the Bible he was using (they don't all have the same ages in Genesis 5 and Genesis 11), but those numbers are certainly in the same ballpark. Exodus to Solomon's Temple The next part is really easy. Per 1 Kings 6:1: In the four hundred eightieth year after the Israelites came out of the land of Egypt, in the fourth year of Solomon’s reign over Israel, in the month of Ziv, which is the second month, he began to build the house of the Lord. So, you've got 480 years from the Exodus until the building of Solomon's Temple. Solomon's Temple to the Babylonian Captivity After that, it takes more effort than I was willing to put into it to trace the reigns of all the kings of Israel and Judah. But just to give a taste, here's 2 Kings 3:1: In the eighteenth year of King Jehoshaphat of Judah, Jehoram son of Ahab became king over Israel in Samaria; he reigned twelve years. So go searching for all those types of verses, and you can work out how long it was until the crowning of king Amel-Marduk. Ussher apparently made some judgment calls on overlapping periods, working out his estimate of 424 years. Somewhat independently, but not nearly as precisely, there are unbroken genealogies in the Gospels from Adam all the way to Jesus. Granted, they do contradict each other, but we'll just look past that. Matthew lists 42 generations from Adam to Jesus, while Luke lists 77. In either case, those give ballpark estimates on the order of thousands of years, even with the unrealistically high generation times in the early books of the Bible. So, the first two portions of that estimate are really pretty straight forward. And they rely on what seem to be matter of fact, boring ancestral lists, not fables, parables, or allegorical moral tales. Sure, it might seem unbelievalbe for a guy to be having kids at 500 years old, but is it really more unbelievable than the Plagues of Egypt or other Bible stories? And the third part, while I didn't go through the numbers, is from the part of the Bible that's actually probably more historically reliable. Even with just the portions I did for myself, if you take those ancestry lists at more or less face value, they get you all the way to Solomon's Temple, going through Egyptian Pharaohs along the way. In the grand scheme of things, that's not that long ago. Assuming for the sake of argument that Solomon and the First Temple really existed, you're looking at a Bronze Age civlization, so somewhere on the order of 1000 BC. So going back 2500 years from that gets you to 3500 BC. So once again, we're in the same ballpark as Ussher. My takeaway after going through all this, is that Ussher was a lot more reasonable than certain quarters of the Internet give him credit for. Sure, you have to accept the Bible as more or less true in the first place. But once you do, his estimate just follows from simple statements of 'fact' within the Bible. Even the slight uncertainties and judgment calls are only on the order of decades (at least for a particular Bible with given numbers) and aren't going to push the dates around all that much. Basically, if you accept Genesis 5 and Genesis 11 as factual, you’ll end up with an estimate somewhere on par with Ussher’s. If you want to reconcile the Bible with the true age of the Earth, you have to explain why Genesis 5 and Genesis 11 aren’t meant to be taken at their word.** *Parts of this answer were adapted and/or copied from a previous answer along similar lines: **And yes. Plenty of Christians do say that Genesis 5 and Genesis 11 aren’t meant to be taken at their word. I’m just pointing out that Ussher was merely following the text.

Could Kamala Harris beat Donald Trump? Yes. And Trump could beat Harris. Presidential elections in the past 30 years have all been relatively close. Roughly half the votes will go to either candidate, plus or minus a few percent that decides who will win (and a few more percent to third party candidates). And of course, that whole process gets filtered through the electoral college, so a candidate doesn't even need a majority of the popular vote to win the election. ABOVE SOURCE: United States presidential election - Wikipedia This year will be no different. Trump will get around half the vote. Harris will get around half the vote. Whoever performs best in the swing states will win the overall election. Sure, you've got plenty of people right now making 'guarantees' about who will win. And given that it's really a binary choice, a lot of those people will inevitably end up picking the eventual winner. But it doesn't mean they actually had any better insight than the rest of us. I think it still is useful and valid as long as you understand it's limitations. It's just that polling can't tell you much when elections are decided by less than the polling margin of error. Can people not understand that the vast majority of religious people accept evolution and all science? That only a small fringe in a few countries with inferior educational systems talk creationist or other science denialist nonsense? No, I don't think you can say that "the vast majority of religious people accept evolution" or that the problem is confined to just "a small fringe in a few countries". Luckily, there’s polling data on this, so let’s take a look. To start off, since it's easiest to find detailed polling data on this for the U.S., here's the data for the U.S. broken down by religion: ABOVE: Pew Results about Human Evolution and Religion from 2018 Poll SOURCE: Data from Religious Landscape Study, Graph redrawn by me Buddhists, Hindus, and Jews all have very high levels of acceptance of evolution – around 80% or higher. That’s probably high enough to consider it a 'vast majority'. But among Christians, Catholics are the group with the most widespread acceptance of evolution, and they're only at 65%, or just under 2/3 acceptance. That's not exactly overwhelming. Evangelical Protestant's and Jehovah's Witnesses are downright hostile towards evolution, with majorities actually supporting creationism. I was able to find similar data for the UK and Canada broken down by religious vs. non-religious: ABOVE: YouGov Results about Human Evolution and Religion from 2017 Poll SOURCE: Data from ScienceReligionSpectrum.org - Resources and Information, Graph redrawn by me Among the religious/spiritual folks in the UK, only 63% supported evolution, while in Canada it was only 54%. Granted, those are majorities, but not vast majorities. For most other countries and regions, I couldn't find quite as detailed of data. It either listed only acceptance rates, or else didn't break things down by religion. At any rate, here are a few of those: ABOVE: Latin American Views on Evolution by Relgion from 2014 Report SOURCE: Pew Forum ABOVE: Views on Evolution in Eastern Europe from 2017 Report SOURCE: Pew Forum, slightly modified by me ABOVE: Worldwide Views on Evolution from 2011 Report SOURCE: Data from Ipsos, Graph by me There are very few countries or regions that I would characterize as having the "vast majority" supporting evolution. Do we actually need to learn about Math at school? Don’t calculators already exist? In my honest opinion, I feel like years of our lives could’ve already been saved if we just used a damn calculator. As I like to somewhat jokingly say, I'm good at math, but not so great with numbers. Calculators handle arithmetic, which is just about the very lowest level of math. You should have mastered that by elementary school and moved on to more advanced math by middle school. At the very least, you should have studied algebra, geometry, and trigonometry by the time you graduated from high school. And even that's barely scratching the surface of the topics you can study in math. As an engineer, I'm nowhere near on par with actual mathematicians, but even I got into topics like calculus, differential equations, and complex numbers. It's kind of like studying language arts. You should have gotten the basics of penmanship and basic literacy in elementary school to form a minimal foundation. Then you move on to more advanced topics as you get older, until eventually you're writing essays and research papers, where you barely even think about the fact that you need to know how to spell or form basic sentences. Such basic tasks are taken for granted. The basic tasks of arithmetic that calculators can handle are the equivalent of being able to write out a sentence. Sure, we've got calculators and Excel for the grunt-work of churning numbers. But you still need an education in math to understand all the concepts behind it to make sense of what your spreadsheet is telling you (and even to build your spreadsheets in the first place). I will grant you something, though. Since calculators and computers are so ubiquitous these days, there isn’t really the need to spend so much time on arithmetic. You still need to understand it at a basic level, but this should free up teachers to start getting into the more advanced and fun topics earlier, so that students can be exposed to more math in the time available in school.

Do atheists believe that cucumbers could evolve into kangaroos if given enough time? Well, I'm not going to say it's flat out impossible, but it does seem very, very unlikely. This is a great example of how historical contingency constrains evolution, since that's not at all the way us animals evolved in the first place. Here's an evolutionary tree of eukaryotes, which is the group that includes both us and plants. Land plants, which includes cucumbers, are in the top left, while us animals (metazoans) are in the bottom left: ABOVE SOURCE: https://bsapubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.3732/ajb.1300314 This figure also shows multicellularity vs. unicellularity vs. colonial species. Based on the pattern, it appears that multicellularity evolved independently in several lineages. Or in other words, our common ancestor with plants was still unicellular, and that we and plants each took a different path to arrive at multicellularity. The lineage that led to plants had already developed photosynthesis before evolving multicellularity, so all of their development towards multicellularity was geared around that lifestyle. Likewise, our single celled ancestors were already consuming other organisms, so all of our development towards multicellularity was geared around that lifestyle. And at this point in the present, our different lineages are specialized for our respective lifestyles. What's more, they're not particularly compatible lifestyles. While sunlight is very plentiful, it's not particularly energy dense compared to eating other organisms. So, plants get by on a lot less energy than us animals, which is part of the reason they tend to be generally immobile (though you do get occasional fast responses like Venus fly traps). By contrast, when we eat a plant, we're basically getting all that energy the plant has stored up over time in just a few bites, before going on to the next plant and the next plant, so we can spend much more energy on things like moving around (not that animals have to move around, as evidenced by sponges). For something like a cucumber to evolve into something like a kangaroo is a drastic, drastic change in how those organisms make a living. Sure, if I get creative enough, I can think of kinda sorta plausible scenarios where it could happen, but truth be told, they don't actually seem genuinely plausible. What's more, as long as existing animals are around, you've got to worry about the competitive exclusion principle. What incipient animal-like plant would be able to outcompete existing actual animals? So yeah, given enough time, I'm not sure you could completely rule out something like this, but it does seem rather unlikely.

Archeologists excavated a fossilised dinosaur, whole, and even found flesh/blood for DNA. Plus carbon-dating, it was proved dinosaurs died SIX MILLION years ago? However, Bible indicates it's been 5776 years now since Adam/Abraham. WHO IS LYING HERE? I'm going to focus on just carbon dating. There are already over 100 other answers to this question covering most everything else, but after skimming several dozen, most just say that carbon dating is only good to about 50k years without giving much of an explanation why. So let me give it a shot. The basis of carbon dating is that there are different isotopes of carbon in the atmosphere. By far the major one is carbon-12 (C12), so named because it has 6 protons and 6 neutrons for a total atomic mass of 12. There is also C13 (6 protons + 7 neutrons), and C14 (6 protons + 8 neutrons). C12 and C13 are stable, meaning that they're not prone to radioactive decay. C14, on the other hand, is radioactive. It will decay with a half life of around 5730 years. That means that every 5730 years, half of what you had will remain. In other words, starting off with 100%, in 5730 years you'll have 50%. In another 5730 years, you'll have half of that, 25%. In another 5730 years, you'll have half of that, 12.5%. This goes on and on until the number of individual atoms gets so small that such probabilistic predictions aren't as useful, anymore. ABOVE SOURCE: Nov. 21 – Halflife and Fission The reason there's C14 in the atmosphere even though it decays is primarily due to cosmic rays. When a cosmic ray impacts a nitrogen-14 (N14) atom in the upper atmosphere, it converts the N14 into an atom of C14. Then, as this C14 diffuses throughout the rest of the atmosphere, it can combine with oxygen to form carbon dioxide (CO2), and eventually get taken up by a plant during photosynthesis. This process has been more or less constant over the past several millennia, so the ratios of C12:C13:C14 have also been more or less constant*. ABOVE SOURCE: SkepticalScience.com - Carbon 14 origin , under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International Although the chemistry of photosynthesis is somewhat biased towards using the lighter isotopes of carbon, plants still take up all of the isotopes, and in proportions that are roughly consistent across all the different kinds of plants (and not too far off from the proportions in the atmosphere – though enough to be measurable). And since most food webs (especially land based ones) have plants at the base, and animals are always eating and pooping and peeing to keep a near constant turnover of their carbon atoms, this same ratio of C12:C13:C14 holds throughout most living things**. However, once an organism dies, it quits taking part in this constant exchange of carbon. The ratio of isotopes will begin to measurably change as the C14 decays. So, knowing the half-life of C14, you can measure this ratio and determine how long it's been since the organism died, i.e. how old it is. (In practice, researchers mostly look at the ratio of C12:C14, and don't pay much attention to C13 – at least for carbon dating – the ratio of C12:C13 is important to environmental scientists and climatologists.) So now we can address the limitations. The first should be rather obvious from the first graph up above. By the time you get something that's been dead for over 50k years, the amount of C14 left is truly miniscule, and real life sensors are only so accurate. In other words, once you get down to such trace levels of C14, you can't expect sensors accurate enough to distinguish between a 100k year old sample and a 150k year old sample. It would be like using a tape measure to try to measure the difference between .001" and .002" – it's simply beyond the capability of the measuring device. Even if you had magic sensors that could count every single atom in a sample, you'd start running into issues of applying probabilities to small sample sizes. As an analogy, consider flipping coins. Flip a coin 1000 times, and you'll almost surely have close to half heads and half tails. Flip a coin 2 times, and 2 heads or 2 tails isn't shocking. Flip a coin 1 time, and you can't have half heads and half tails. If I did my math right, a 1g sample of carbon would contain around 5e22 atoms. Given the ratio of C12 to C14, that would be around 5.7e10 (57 trillion) C14 atoms. With a half life of 5730 years, the math works out to 1.65 atoms in just over 200,000 years. Obviously, you can't have 1.65 atoms. But more fundamentally, at such small sample sizes, you don't know if an individual atom will decay tomorrow, or in another 100,000 years. So when you're left with just a handful of atoms, random chance can outweigh probability. ABOVE SOURCE: Me and Excel And there's another problem on top of that. Just because most of the C14 comes from cosmic rays doesn't mean that all of it does. Cosmic rays aren't the only source of the high energy particles that can convert N14 into C14. The decay of the uranium-thorium isotope series also releases such particles that can accomplish the same conversion. And since there are trace levels of uranium basically throughout the entire planet, along with deposits with higher concentrations, this process will occur pretty much everywhere. In living and relatively recently deceased organisms, the trace amounts of C14 from such other sources is dwarfed by that from the atmosphere, so that the effect on dating is negligible. But once a sample is old enough that most of the C14 that originally came from the atmosphere has already decayed, that sample will still contain newly created C14 from background radiation. Or alternatively, even objects that were never alive and never had any atmospheric C14 could have some level of C14 from these other sources. So, those are the issues with trying to apply carbon dating to objects older than around 50k years. I mean, sure, you can go through the procedures, and an algorithm might even spit out a number. But that number is meaningless. It doesn't really tell you anything about the age of such an object. You certainly can’t get a meaningful number from carbon dating*** for an object millions of years old. *By calibrating carbon dating to other dating methods like tree ring counting, researchers discovered that the ratios of C12:C13:C14 weren't exactly constant over the past tens of thousands of years, allowing them to come up with calibration curves to give more precise dates. **Certain ecosystems, such as those deep underwater in the ocean, are more isolated from atmospheric C14, and so may have different ratios. So you should only apply carbon dating to samples from organisms that lived in or near the atmosphere. ***Thankfully, there are other radioisotope dating methods, but these are applied to igneous or volcanic rocks and ash, and so date the sediment above and below objects of interest, not the objects themselves. Different radioactive substances with different half lives have different useful ranges.

And I know that specifically because we had a full house of relatives who were in town for her quinceañera. Our doggie/cat door was from the house to the garage. We then left the small back door of the garage open to the back yard, so that the cats and weenie dog could get in and out that way. We'd occasionally had issues with racoons in the past when I kept the dog food out in the garage, but after I started securing the lid better, they started leaving us alone. But that evening, we'd left the big garage door open, and a family of racoons got into the garage. We thought we'd chased them all out, so we completely shut all the outside garage doors, thinking that would keep the entire family out. Sometime around two in the morning, the weenie dog started barking and barking, waking up everybody in the house. I came downstairs, and there he was, with a baby racoon cornered in the family room and a gathering crowd of family members. I guess one of the racoon family had been left behind and found its way through the doggie door. My uncle told me it was just a baby so why don't I just go and grab it. I shot back why doesn't he go grab it. In the end, we called animal control, and they came and got it. A Nosy Neighbor We went for years without any more unexpected visitors to the house. In the meantime, our previous cats and dogs had all died, and we'd become roommates with a new cat, who started off feral using our garage, and who I was able to eventually coax into the house and teach him how to use the cat door. My wife named him Chester. He was a long haired tabby cat. There was another long haired tabby cat running around the neighborhood who looked very similar. At first, I named this other cat Not Chester. But I eventually learned that he was an actual pet who belonged to our neighbor two houses down, who we then began calling Sir William Wallace the Gentleman. Well, being a house cat himself, he understood the concept of cat doors, and I began catching him, or evidence of him, in the house on a pretty regular basis. It was especially irritating to find the butter I left out on the counter with a whole bunch of cat sized bites taken out. The last straw was when I was in our upstairs office working from home, and he had the audacity to come all the way upstairs to the room I was in. After that, I investigated higher tech options, and bought an electronic cat flap that you could program to only unlock for your specific cat's RFID chip (which meant Chester also got a trip to the vet to get chipped). Problem solved, mostly. A Thief in the Night One problem with this cat flap is that the way it locked under normal operation, it only blocked the flap from opening inward. For going out, the flap could still swing open. This worked fine for most animals, but racoons aren't most animals. We had a container full of pecans in the dining room, close to the garage door, and I came down one morning to find pecan shells all over the dining room floor. I didn't think too much about it, and just cleaned them up. But when it happened again, I knew there was a problem. It seems that the racoon had figured out how to get just enough of a grip on the flap to pull it open from the outside. Somewhat fortuitously, that was just around the time I was getting ready to head to El Paso for a month, taking Chester with me. So I set the cat flap to the completely locked mode (which wouldn't open in either direction), and put a trash can right in front of it on the inside of the house. I think the racoon figured out that his free meal ticket was over, so that seemed to put an end to it. Still a Nosy Neighbor Now that we've had the electronic flap for a couple years, it doesn't swing quite as freely as it did when new. So sometimes when Chester comes in, it won't swing back all the way shut to where it gets locked. And so, just a month or two ago, I was downstairs with Chester on my lap, when I heard something eating his cat food. I looked, and there was Sir William Wallace stealing Chester's food. So I chased him out again. So yeah, we've had our share of uninvited guests thanks to the doggie/cat door. The electronic one seems to have solved most of the problems, but it hasn't stopped them completely.

Is English considered a foreign language to the US? Why can't most Americans speak English fluently or even close? As someone who has been learning English for about 3 months, I probably speak much better English than most Americans. Why? I'm going to focus on this part of your question: As someone who has been learning English for about 3 months, I probably speak much better English than most Americans. No, you don't. I studied Spanish pretty extensively in high school and college, to the point of being only 2 classes away from a Spanish minor*. I could speak fairly fluently. Then, after I graduated, I met the woman who was to become my wife, who happens to be Mexican with a large Mexican family (all living in the U.S.). I could catch them making grammatical 'errors' that weren't 'proper' Spanish**, and I could definitely spell Spanish words better than them (they mostly grew up in the U.S., so didn't have much formal education in Spanish). But my way of speaking Spanish was much more academic and stuffy, and just didn't flow the same way. Nobody would have confused me as speaking better Spanish than native speakers who had been speaking it their entire lives. Going the other way, I once made a business trip to China, and during the one day we set aside for sight seeing, I was approached by an old Chinese guy who wanted to speak to me in English, who turned out to be a retired English teacher. In other words, he was such an expert in the English language among the Chinese that he was teaching others how to speak English. But his English wasn't exactly the best. Don't get me wrong, his English was far better than my non-existent skills in Chinese, but it seemed obvious that he'd probably never been outside China and gotten to practice with actual native speakers. Even a lifetime of academic study isn't enough to make someone speak as well as a native speaker. Now, I really suspect you're a troll and not somebody who just began studying English 3 months ago. But people who aren't native speakers have to study a long, long, long time to become as proficient at the language as native speakers. And it really requires immersion in the culture, hearing the language day in and day out to pick up all the nuances and informalities that you simply can't completely learn any other way. On the off chance that you really are new to studying English, learn a bit of humility like I did when I met my wife’s family. Academic English is not the way real people speak, and it’s going to take a lot more than three months of studying in a school environment before you sound natural. *The reason I didn't just tack on two more classes was because I was already taking one Spanish class my final semester, and another two would have given me a very full load. So, instead, I tacked on a semester of Italian to learn a bit more of a different language. I figured the actual skill would serve me better than an additional piece of paper. **I put grammatical 'errors' in scare quotes, because I've come around to the idea of grammar being descriptive, not prescriptive. Who gets to decide what's proper and what's not. Where do they get off thinking they have that authority? Language has been around for far longer than scholars to study it, and people did just fine.

Where does the concept of the Earth being six thousand years old come from? Is it from the Bible? It really does come from the Bible, if a bit indirectly. There are several passages in the Bible that give information on such things as how old people were when they had children or how long certain periods lasted, that if accepted at face value, can give a very close approximation of when Adam and Eve were created (according to the stories, at least). There are a few places where things get somewhat murky, but not enough to change things by more than a few decades* – nothing on the order of millions or billions of years. This was a fairly well accepted interpretation for generations, and many scholars made their own estimates of when creation would have taken place, including Johannes Kepler. Arguably the most respected of these was the estimate done by James Ussher, who put much effort into sorting out the murky periods. It's because Ussher's chronology was so well respected that it was included in the introductory material to several printed Bibles, including the famed Scofield Bible. Wikipedia gives a good summary of how Ussher made his estimate (Ussher chronology - Wikipedia). He broke it down into three periods: Using other sources outside the Bible, Ussher determined the enthronement of the Babylonian king Amel-Marduk to have occurred in 562 BC, which was tied in to the end of the Babylonian Captivity through 2 Kings 25:27. From there, it was just a matter of going backwards by all the years previously calculated, putting creation at 4004 BC. Creation to Exodus You can easily look up Genesis 5 and Genesis 11 for yourself, but to give an idea, here's the start of Genesis 5: This is the list of the descendants of Adam. When God created humans,[a] he made them[b] in the likeness of God. 2 Male and female he created them, and he blessed them and called them humans[c] when they were created. 3 When Adam had lived one hundred thirty years, he became the father of a son in his likeness, according to his image, and named him Seth. 4 The days of Adam after he became the father of Seth were eight hundred years, and he had other sons and daughters. 5 Thus all the days that Adam lived were nine hundred thirty years, and he died. 6 When Seth had lived one hundred five years, he became the father of Enosh. 7 Seth lived after the birth of Enosh eight hundred seven years and had other sons and daughters. 8 Thus all the days of Seth were nine hundred twelve years, and he died. It goes on and on like that. So, as long as you accept these statements as true, it's mostly a simple matter of adding up how old each man was when he begat his heir. The only real hiccups are between Noah and Shem, and between Nahor and Terah. Both of these are somewhat ambiguous. In the former, the passage states, "After Noah was five hundred years old, Noah became the father of Shem, Ham, and Japheth." In the latter, the passage is, "When Terah had lived seventy years, he became the father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran." People who care about this issue more than I do have gone into detail to try to pinpoint those ages (e.g. Contradictions: Noah’s Three Sons). You also need to know how old Abraham was when the Exodus occurred. His age at the start of all those events comes from Genesis 12:4, "So Abram went, as the Lord had told him, and Lot went with him. Abram was seventy-five years old when he departed from Haran." I ran the math myself with a spreadsheet, and came up with 2049 years from the creation of Adam to the birth of Abraham, plus another 75 years until the Exodus, for 2124 years total (a bit different from Ussher because I didn't put in the effort to figure out the ambiguity around Noah/Shem and Nahor/Terah). I suppose there's one other hiccup, depending on which particular version of the Bible you're using. Since we don't have an 'original' version of Genesis, we have to rely on copies of that version, most notably the Masoretic text and the Septuagint (though those aren't the only two). And those copies differ on certain details, including all those ages in Genesis 5 and Genesis 11. Exodus to Solomon's Temple Like I said, this one comes straight from a single verse, 1 Kings 6:1: In the four hundred eightieth year after the Israelites came out of the land of Egypt, in the fourth year of Solomon’s reign over Israel, in the month of Ziv, which is the second month, he began to build the house of the Lord. Solomon's Temple to the Babylonian Captivity This is the period where things purportedly get a bit more complicated. I haven't gone through this period in detail, yet, myself, but to give just one example, you have this verse from 2 Kings 3:1: In the eighteenth year of King Jehoshaphat of Judah, Jehoram son of Ahab became king over Israel in Samaria; he reigned twelve years. Go through finding all those verses and work out the years, and you come up a little over 4 centuries of history. In a somewhat independent path, other books in the Bible also give more genealogies, such that you can trace each and every claimed descendant from Adam all the way to Jesus. Granted, there aren't ages associated with all of those genealogies, but these also give a ballpark range in the thousands of years. So, if you accept the claims of the Bible at more or less face value, and assume all those genealogies represent real people and not just imaginary people made up out of thin air, and that all the events in Egypt, Israel, and Judah all really happened, you'll end up at an estimate for the date of creation somewhere around 4000 BC. As a side note, while it seems to be somewhat fashionable to dismiss exercises like these because some parts of the Bible were ‘obviously’ meant to be taken more metaphorically or allegorically, I don’t see such figurative interpretations as obvious at all. The crux of this argument would be the genealogies in Genesis 5 and Genesis 11 – after that, you’re already into Egyptian pharaohs, so nothing that’s going to be a major difference from real history (at least as far as timelines). But these genealogies aren’t fables with moral lessons or some type of simplified explanation of complex concepts for a pre-scientific society. They’re boring, dry lists of ancestry. It’s about as close to a conventional history section as you’ll find in Genesis – the part least likely to be metaphorical or allegorical (though there’s certainly a reason to ‘invent’ such lists to provide legitimacy for the rulers of Israel and Judah). *As I already touched upon, that difference of only a few decades is using a specific version of the Bible, such as the Masoretic text or the Septuagint. The differences between those different versions can add up to a couple millennia, though still not anywhere near on the magnitude of real history.

Why can't English rugby be as popular as American football in the USA? Well, they started off from the same roots, but then developed along independent paths in their respective countries. So it's no wonder that the version that developed in the USA is more popular in the USA. Both rugby and gridiron football, along with the various other types of football, grew out of a family of British games known as mob football, with different 'house rules' among every group in every town and village that played it. Since it was British colonists who were the first Europeans to come to what would become the U.S. and Canada, they brought along their British sports, including mob football. Round about the mid 1800s, social conditions were finally ripe to begin formalizing these diverse rules with different governing bodies. At the time, the Rugby School's rules were very similar to the rules at several American and Canadian colleges like Harvard, McGill, and Yale (in contrast to the association football rules of Cambridge and the Sheffield Football Club). The New World teams went on to develop new innovations that moved the sport further away from its cousin, rugby, including the line of scrimmage, a system of downs, and then in 1906 the forward pass (Walter Camp was especially influential in many of these innovations). ABOVE: An 1895 football game between Auburn and Georgia looking a lot more like rugby than modern day gridiron football SOURCE: College football - Wikipedia ABOVE: Another pre-forward pass college football game – the University of Minnesota vs. the University of Michigan in 1902 SOURCE: College football - Wikipedia So basically, the two sports started off largely the same, but then went down separate paths in each country. So of course the rules that developed in the USA are more popular here. If most Americans had wanted to play a game more similar to rugby, they wouldn't have changed the rules in the first place.

Why is there a theory to evolution? Because that’s how science works. Theories are the high level frameworks we use to study things. In my own field of aerospace engineering, for example, let’s say I wanted to analyze a propeller. For a back of the envelope type analysis, I could use momentum theory. If I want to dig a little deeper, I could use blade element theory. If I want to go even further, I could use computational fluid dynamics. So, I’ve got at least three different theories I can use to analyze the same thing (with many different levels of implementation even within each of those theories). Evolution’s the same way. We know it happens, but there are different ways of looking at it and different theories you can use to study it. The over-arching high level theory is the modern synthesis or the extended synthesis, but there are sub-parts to that, many of which could be considered theories in their own right: ABOVE SOURCE: Epigenetic opportunities for Evolutionary Computation And off the top of my head, even that figure is leaving out lower level concepts like genetic drift, neutral theory, Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, etc. Basically, there are theories to evolution, because evolution is science, and science uses theories.
