Why do liberals claim to be Christians? They support abortion, homosexual marriage, etc. These people do not follow any of the Bible's rules, why do they still call themselves Christians? There is a word "heresy" and it applies to liberals While I'm no longer a Christian, I was raised as one. And frankly, liberal political positions seem to be far more consistent with the Christian values I was taught. Let's start with the two you mentioned, and then look more at the core of Jesus's teachings. Abortion Plenty of other answers have already discussed how there's not really much Biblical basis for the modern day anti-abortion movement, including citing specific chapter and verse to show that the Bible implicitly doesn't value a fetus as much as a person. So, instead of repeating all that here, I'll just point you to one of those answers: I do want to call attention to something else, however, that even as recently as the 1970s, conservative Christians weren't as extreme as they are today, and that this is largely due to an intentional political strategy to embrace abortion as a rallying issue for the right wing. There's a good article at The Conversation about the shifting views on abortion among Southern Baptists: Many Southern Baptists saw opposition to abortion as more of a Catholic issue. And while the Southern Baptist Convention didn't support unfettered access to abortion for any reason at all, "a majority of Southern Baptist pastors supported abortion in a number of instances, including when the woman’s mental or physical health was at risk or in the case of rape or fetal deformity." And when Roe v. Wade was decided, many Southern Baptists were actually happy with the outcome. Quoting that article once again, "many Southern Baptists saw the Roe decision as drawing a needed line between church and state on matters of morality and state regulation. A Baptist Press article just days after the decision called it an advancement of religious liberty, human equality and justice." How many modern day Southern Baptists do you think would praise Roe v. Wade that way? Anyway, the point is that the modern day extremism of anti-choice folks doesn't really have much of a Biblical basis, and there have been and remain plenty of different views among Christians regarding abortion, and especially what role government and legislation should play in the issue. Marriage I remember when our Catholic priest found out my parents had been married in a Lutheran church. He said something to the effect of, 'You mean you're not married?' He insisted that they get married through the Catholic sacrament so that their marriage could be 'real'. But that's the thing about living in a multi-cultural society. It doesn't matter if my priest thought that Lutheran, Baptist, or Hindu marriages were illegitimate in the eyes of God. For the secular purposes of the state, marriage is just a legal agreement between two people. And it really takes very little effort to extend that to same sex couples. Or to put it another way, if we already allow 'sinful' marriages between people of 'false' religions, why is same sex marriage any different? Nobody is forcing you or your church to change your religious ceremonies. They're just not letting you force your own religion on others. For what it's worth, that was exactly my position when I was still a Christian – I was personally opposed to same sex marriage from a moral standpoint, but wanted it to be legal since I couldn't see any secular reason not to. Or to take a far less controversial example, I didn’t expect government to outlaw consumption of meat on Fridays during Lent. That was something that I practiced, not something to be forced on others. Marriage was the same way. What I wanted for my own marriage as a Christian was not something to be forced onto society at large through law. Jesus's Core Message At least per the Gospels, Jesus actually told his followers which commandments were the most important. I'm guessing that if you're a Christian, you already know this, but just to be thorough, here's the relevant passage from Matthew 22 (emphasis mine): When the Pharisees heard that he had silenced the Sadducees, they gathered together, and one of them, an expert in the law, asked him a question to test him. “Teacher, which commandment in the law is the greatest?” He said to him, “ ‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind.’ This is the greatest and first commandment. And a second is like it: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ On these two commandments hang all the Law and the Prophets.” For this answer, I want to highlight the second one, there, because that one has more implications on how people should be treating other people. In Luke 10, in a similar passage where Jesus preached the importance of loving your neighbor as yourself, he was asked a follow-up question of "And who is my neighbor?" Of course, this is where Jesus responded with the famous parable of the Good Samaritan, which culminated with this lesson: Which of these three, do you think, was a neighbor to the man who fell into the hands of the robbers?” He said, “The one who showed him mercy.” Jesus said to him, “Go and do likewise.” And of course, there's another famous parable from Matthew 25: Then the king will say to those at his right hand, ‘Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world, for I was hungry and you gave me food, I was thirsty and you gave me something to drink, I was a stranger and you welcomed me, I was naked and you gave me clothing, I was sick and you took care of me, I was in prison and you visited me.’ Then the righteous will answer him, ‘Lord, when was it that we saw you hungry and gave you food or thirsty and gave you something to drink? And when was it that we saw you sick or in prison and visited you?’ And the king will answer them, ‘Truly I tell you, just as you did it to one of the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did it to me.’ Jesus preached caring for the hungry, the poor, the strangers in our midst, and even prisoners. And there weren't caveats about nationality. In all honesty, which political party in the U.S. has more support for these types of social programs, for our own citizens, refugees arriving at our borders, and international aid to the least of our brothers and sisters around the world?
